title: Herod's Temple
hook: a hard king rebuilds the Temple, and one of its great outer walls still stands

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dead Sea Scrolls: old words kept in the dark near the Dead Sea until they were found again. Your line was hidden in caves. Did something tucked away turn up for you? Today a new part of the story opens: Rome, destruction, and the rabbis. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

Folded slips of paper, pushed into the cracks between huge pale stones. Small green plants growing out of the joints. Some people press their foreheads to the stone. Some stand back and read psalms from a small book. Some just lay a hand flat on the wall and stay a while. This is the Western Wall in Jerusalem, in Hebrew the Kotel. It isn't the Temple itself. It's part of the great outer wall that held up the platform the Temple once stood on. To understand why people come to a retaining wall to pray, go back to the man who had it built. His name was Herod.
screen: `PAPERS IN THE CRACKS.` → `NOT THE TEMPLE, BUT ITS WALL.` → `GO BACK TO HEROD.`

segments.voice: Herod was a king of Judea who ruled with Rome's backing. The Jewish historian Josephus tells his story in detail, and it isn't gentle. Herod was suspicious and violent; Josephus records that he had members of his own family put to death. And this same king set out to rebuild the Second Temple, the house that had stood since the return from Babylon. Josephus describes the hill being enlarged, enormous walls raised around it to hold up a wide, level court, and a sanctuary so covered in gold and white stone that from far off it looked like a snowy mountain. The rabbis of the Talmud tell a harder story about how it began. In the tractate Bava Batra, Herod has killed the sages. One survives, Bava ben Buta, whom Herod has blinded. Herod, in disguise, tries to trick him into cursing the king. He won't. Herod then asks him what a man like himself could do to make amends, and the old sage answers, in paraphrase: you darkened the light of the world, so go and tend the light of the world. Rebuild the Temple. And the same page keeps a saying, in paraphrase: whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building. A cruel king. A beautiful house. The rabbis keep both facts and smooth over neither. The sanctuary itself would not last. But part of the western retaining wall did. One midrash reads a line from the Song of Songs, "behold, he standeth behind our wall", and says God's presence never leaves the Western Wall. The Hebrew word for wall in that verse is the same word people use for the Kotel.
screen: `A HARD KING REBUILDS THE TEMPLE.` · `A BLINDED SAGE SAYS: TEND THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `NEVER SEEN A BEAUTIFUL BUILDING.` · then: `"BEHIND OUR WALL."`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at the wall. Close your eyes and hold the scene, or, if a screen is nearby, find a picture of the Western Wall: big pale stones, a few plants in the joints, folded papers tucked between. Pick one stone and stay with it. Someone cut it for Herod. Many hands have touched it since. Let your breath slow while you look. Then think of one thing in your own life that remained after something larger was gone: a recipe that outlived a kitchen, a habit someone taught you, a photograph. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know, the way people do at the wall. The bell holds the time.
Herod's Temple. Rebuilt by a hard king, praised even by the rabbis who remembered his cruelty, and part of its western wall still stands. Today's word.
Your line: the wall remains. Today, notice one thing that outlasted something bigger, and give it a moment of your attention. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Jews pray at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, and visitors leave folded written prayers in the cracks between its stones.

fork.setup: you're Bava ben Buta. the king who blinded you asks how he can make amends. what do you say?
options: curse him and refuse to answer.
tell him to rebuild the Temple.
tell him to leave Jerusalem forever.
fork.reveal: in the Talmud's story, the sage won't curse the king. he tells him to tend the light of the world by rebuilding the Temple, and Herod does.

original.note: Hebrew: wall, the everyday name for the Western Wall in Jerusalem.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old wall people visit in Jerusalem.
what it means: part of the retaining wall of the Temple Mount that a cruel king rebuilt on a grand scale, still standing after the sanctuary fell.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud keeps Herod's cruelty and his beautiful building on the same page, and a midrash reads "behind our wall" as God's presence never leaving the Western Wall.
